_purpose: Cross-judge calibration for the specificity score, measured on PAIRED data: skills scored by both judges from identical bytes. Retrieval should apply the offset before comparing specificity across the Luna-outage window, and should respect the noise floor when using specificity as a ranking key.
_method: For every norm_hash with an is_real_skill=true primary verdict from BOTH gpt-5.6-luna@medium and claude-haiku-4-5-20251001/primary-failover, take haiku_specificity - luna_specificity. Paired on identical content, so the comparison is not confounded by which skills each judge happened to see -- the unpaired means suggested a -0.10 gap, which was wrong.

claude-haiku-4-5-20251001/primary-failov._note: Add 0.05 to a failover-window specificity score to put it on the Luna scale.

noise_floor._implication: Two judges reading the SAME bytes disagree with a standard deviation of ~0.107, and agree within 0.05 only 36% of the time. Specificity therefore cannot support fine-grained ranking -- a 0.88 vs 0.85 difference is noise, not signal. Use coarse bands instead. The bands measured in exp_marginal_value.py do carry real signal: skills below 0.75 add genuinely new information 55% of the time versus ~77% for everything above it, a 22-point gap that survives this noise.
noise_floor.recommended_use: Three bands (<0.75, 0.75-0.9, >=0.9) as a coarse prior on informativeness. Not a sort key.

_caveats: 102 pairs is enough to establish the offset's sign and rough size, not to pin it to two decimals.
The offset is measured only for the primary-failover snapshot. Any future judge change needs its own paired measurement before its scores are mixed with these.
Verdicts are NOT rewritten in place. The stored score always reflects what the judge actually said; correction is applied at read time so provenance survives and this constant can be revised.
